Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text:
h02.

**Delivery function — `Post` in `internal/webhook/webhook.go:120`; protection mechanism — `safeDialContext` / `isReservedIP` in `internal/webhook/webhook.go:59` backed by `internal/webhook/validate.go:44`.**

**Where delivery executes**

- `webhook.Post` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:120`) does the real work: marshals the payload, builds the `POST`, adds Standard Webhooks HMAC headers (`webhook-id` / `webhook-timestamp` / `webhook-signature`) when a signing secret is set, then issues the request via `safeClient.Do` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:152`) and validates the response body/status.
- Callers never call `Post` directly. `webhook.PostAsync` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:184`) enqueues onto a buffered channel (`asyncPostQueue`, cap 128, `webhook.go:39`), drained by 4 goroutines started in `init()` (`webhook.go:42-55`) that call `Post`. Overflow is dropped with a warning, not blocked.
- Trigger points are `server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go:43` and `:71` (memo created/updated/deleted and comment-created dispatchers), which fan out over each user's stored webhooks.

**What protects it from internal addresses** — two layers:

1. **Dial-time enforcement (the real guard).** `safeClient`'s `Transport.DialContext` is `safeDialContext` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:32-37`, defined at `:59`). It splits host/port, resolves the host itself, and rejects the connection if *any* resolved IP satisfies `isReservedIP`. Because the check happens at dial time on every connection, it also defeats DNS rebinding — a host that validated cleanly at save time can't later resolve to an internal address.
2. **Admission-time validation.** `webhook.ValidateURL` (`internal/webhook/validate.go:62`) is called when a user creates or updates a webhook (`server/router/api/v1/user_service_webhooks.go:74`, `:161`, `:182`). It requires an absolute `http`/`https` URL and rejects hostnames resolving into reserved ranges, returning a gRPC `InvalidArgument`.

The blocklist is `reservedCIDRs` (`internal/webhook/validate.go:14-23`): IPv4 loopback, all three RFC-1918 ranges, `169.254.0.0/16` (covers the cloud IMDS at 169.254.169.254), plus IPv6 `::1/128`, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`. Parsed once at startup into `reservedNetworks` (`validate.go:28-36`).

Two things worth flagging:

- `AllowPrivateIPs` (`internal/webhook/validate.go:41`) is a global kill switch — when true, `isReservedIP` returns false unconditionally and *both* layers go away. Grepping the tree, nothing ever assigns it outside its declaration, so it's currently dead-off (defaults to `false`); it's a hook for self-hosted deployments with no wiring to a flag or config yet.
- The CIDR list doesn't cover `0.0.0.0/8`, carrier-grade NAT `100.64.0.0/10`, or IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), so those aren't blocked by `isReservedIP` as written.
